# Rays sweep their way past Yankees to reach 3rd ALCS in franchise history

October 8th, 2026

Adam Berry

NEW YORK -- Two weeks ago, Kevin Cash set the tone for the rowdy celebration raging in the visitors' clubhouse at Yankee Stadium with a message that made it clear the Rays weren’t done. They had accomplished their regular-season goals, getting back to the postseason and winning their first American League East title in five years, but that wasn’t the end.

They had more in mind. Eleven more wins. Three more chances to pop champagne, pour out bottles of beer, smoke cigars, sing and dance together.

The Rays took another big step toward their ultimate goal on Wednesday night at Yankee Stadium, capping a sweep of the Yankees with a 4-3 victory in Game 3 of the AL Division Series, then once again turned the clubhouse at Yankee Stadium into their bar, lounge and dance floor.

Three wins down, eight more to go.

“We're loving it, man. We want to keep going,” a shirtless and soaked Nick Martinez said amid the celebration. “Like Cashy said, there's two more bites on the bone for us, and we know it. We know what's at stake. We know we want to keep playing.”​

Game 1 of the AL Championship Series is set for Monday at Tropicana Field, with the Rays hosting the winner of the Guardians-White Sox series that Chicago currently leads, 2-1.

The Rays earned their spot by completing the first sweep in a best-of-five postseason series (or longer) in franchise history, and they dealt the Yankees only their second sweep (alongside the 1980 ALCS) in a best-of-five series.

“Very special. Not an easy feat,” Martinez said. “Again, [the Yankees are] a very dangerous team. It's great to not have to play another game because you don't want to leave a team like that hanging around.”

Recognizing the work ahead of them, the Rays made sure they savored the moment. 

A year to the day after their ownership group’s introductory press conference at George M. Steinbrenner Field, Rays managing partner Patrick Zalupski, co-chair Bill Cosgrove and CEO Ken Babby stood on the edge of the fray and smiled. Nearly the entire roster took part in a choreographed dance in the clubhouse. Players sang and danced to Jay-Z’s “Empire State of Mind” and Frank Sinatra’s “Theme from New York, New York” rang through the sound system.

“I love drinking beer, and I love popping bottles. That's what it comes down to. I love it,” outfielder Ryan Vilade said. “This team is so special. We play for one another. We love each other, and we're not done. We don't want it to end.”

When Cash made his way through the stadium’s lower-level tunnel and sat behind a table for his postgame press conference, he looked shockingly dry considering the state of the group he’d just walked away from. There was a reason for that.

“This is my second shirt, second hat,” he quipped. “I've changed it twice.”

None of this was expected of the Rays. They were widely picked to finish last in the AL East. Even as they spent much of the season atop the AL standings, observers singled out other contenders as the league’s “team to beat.” But they proved themselves throughout the 162-game marathon, and they handily beat the AL’s second-best team in a three-game sprint by playing their game.

They pitched well. They played clean defense. And their dynamic lineup showed it can score in a bunch of different ways.

“They're a team by every definition. Every sense of the word 'team,' it's there. I've never seen anything like it,” president of baseball operations Erik Neander said. “These guys care so much for one another, and you want to win for so many reasons: the community, the team, it's our job. But man, for this group, you want them to do it that much more. 

“You want to see them have these moments because of the way they've come together, and they deserve it.”

Yankees lose ALDS 2026

# 'It's a failure': Yankees' championship drought extended to 17 seasons

October 8th, 2026

Bryan Hoch

NEW YORK – There was no team meeting held, no rah-rah speech offered in the clubhouse as the first pitch approached on Wednesday night. Their backs against the wall, these Yankees understood the stakes: Play well for the next nine innings, or endure another long winter filled with questions.

The Yankees prepared and spoke as though they were not ready to let their season end. Despite those intentions, their championship hopes expired with a 4-3 loss to the Rays in Game 3 of the American League Division Series, with the Bronx hosting yet another visitors’ celebration.

“As far as I’m concerned, it’s a failure since we weren’t able to get the job done,” said Ben Rice. “It’s on to next year, unfortunately. … They outplayed us, plain and simple. They outpitched us, out-hit us. It’s really that simple.”

After 93 regular-season victories and a lopsided sweep of the Red Sox in the AL Wild Card Series, what manager Aaron Boone described as his “broken clubhouse” will spend the rest of October as observers, the franchise’s World Series drought now extended to 17 seasons as a 2009 parade through the Canyon of Heroes fades further into memory.

“We’ve got to be more complete offensively, defensively, pitching,” Boone said. “We did really good things this year, but ultimately not good enough to beat a really good Rays team.”

Max Fried surrendered a go-ahead home run to Victor Mesa Jr. on his final pitch, a hanging sixth-inning sweeper that landed in the seats. But the more memorable play was the homer that wasn’t – what initially appeared to be an Anthony Volpe game-tying home run over Mesa’s head in left field.

Mesa immediately pointed into the crowd, where the ball had struck a man’s hands. A crew chief review determined spectator interference on the play, as one replay angle showed the fan reaching past the wall. George Lombard Jr. was awarded home plate, and Volpe was credited with a double.

The crowd of 48,865 howled, and after debris was cleared from the warning track, Spencer Jones struck out to end the inning.

“We were expecting to move on,” Volpe said. “If they beat us down and we had no shot, in some ways it’d probably be better.”

The Yankees never held a lead across 27 ALDS innings, swept in a best-of-five series for the second time in franchise history. The other time was in the 1980 AL Championship Series, won by the Royals.

For the second time in 15 days, Yankee Stadium’s visitors clubhouse was filled by a Rays party – this time, toasting their advance into the ALCS, awaiting the conclusion of the White Sox-Guardians ALDS.

“We don’t like that, other teams celebrating in our place,” said captain Aaron Judge, who was inactive for the postseason. “But if you don’t like it, you’ve got to play better.”

Much like the Blue Jays a year ago, the Rays were a problem the Yankees never seemed able to solve, finishing 4 1/2 games behind in the AL East and losing seven of their 13 regular-season meetings.

Tampa Bay’s reputation for buttoned-up play shone through: The Rays ran the bases aggressively and pressured the Yankees’ defense.

Those differences were more pronounced in the ALDS, however, especially in the series-opening games at Tropicana Field. The Yankees were held to one hit in Game 1, then committed four errors in a Game 2 loss, falling for the seventh time in nine games at Tropicana Field this season (including the playoffs).

“We gave them some room to breathe, and they took it and ran with it,” said Lombard Jr. “It hurts. It sucks. But we’re going to have to learn from it and not let it happen next year.”

New York erased a pair of early deficits in Game 3, punching back after Tampa Bay delivered the first blows. Rice lined a run-scoring single facing Nick Martinez in the third inning, and Jones greeted Ian Seymour with an RBI double in the fourth.

## Tampa Bay advances to its first ALCS since 2020, setting up a Monday opener against Chicago or Cleveland and extending New York's championship drought to 17 seasons.

 By AP 

 Oct 8, 2026 at 1:56 am ET • 5 min read 

NEW YORK (AP) Victor Mesa Jr. didn't bother to watch his home run land in Yankee Stadium's right-field seats, instead turning to his Tampa Bay teammates in the third base dugout.

Rays manager Kevin Cash waved an arm and pointed toward first base, urging Mesa to start the type of trot the 25-year-old yearned of when he defected from Cuba in 2018.

“That’s the moment that you want to live when you’re growing up,” Mesa said after his tiebreaking, two-run homer off Max Fried in the sixth inning lifted Tampa Bay over the New York Yankees 4-3 on Wednesday night for a three-game sweep of their AL Division Series.

Ryan Vilade also homered for the Rays, who got help from a fan interference call and reached the American League Championship Series for the first time since 2020. They host the Chicago White Sox or Cleveland Guardians in the opener on Monday.

“We’re a bunch of dogs,” Vilade said. “We don’t care who’s on the other side. We’re going to go out and compete and do our thing.”

Mesa, 25, was designated for assignment by Miami just ahead of spring training, then traded to the Rays.

“Look where I am now," he said.

Cash had worried when Mesa lingered at home plate.

“The last thing we need to do is ignite a really great team over there,” the manager said of the Yankees. “I get the emotions and the excitement and that was probably the biggest home run he’s ever hit in his life, so I totally appreciate how you want to enjoy that. In today’s game, there's a fine line of what’s OK and what’s not.”

A son of former Cuba player and national team manager Victor Mesa, Victor Jr. was 16 when he left Cuba along with his older brother, Victor Victor Mesa. Both signed with the Miami Marlins and the older brother didn't advance past Triple-A.

“When we defect(ed), we knew that we wanted to live moments like this," Victor Mesa Jr. said. “I want to thank him because he’s a big part of why I’m here.”

Vilade, 27, is with his sixth major league organization and got extensive big league playing time for the first time this season.

“Last year I was in Memphis and sleeping on an Amazon - or a Walmart bed,” he said of his stint with St. Louis' Triple-A farm team. “And this year I’m here and get to go to the ALCS and compete with my guys.”

After Mesa's homer gave the Rays a 4-2 lead, Anthony Volpe appeared to hit a two-run shot against Griffin Jax with two outs in the bottom half as a fan reached over the left-field wall and caught the ball over the glove of a leaping Mesa.

A video review by replay umpire Malachi Moore determined the ball would not have been over the wall and would not have been caught by Mesa. Volpe was awarded an RBI double and George Lombard Jr. was allowed to score from first base. Jax recovered to strike out Spencer Jones.

Baseball's embrace of video technology was key to the inning.

Lombard reached with a one-out walk when a 3-1 pitch called a strike by plate umpire Dan Bellino was ruled inside on an ABS challenge. Austin Wells then walked on full-count changeup but an ABS challenge by Rays catcher Liam Hicks ruled the pitch caught the inside corner for a strikeout, bringing up Volpe.

Quite a change from 1996, when umpires did not have replays to assist and Derek Jeter's homer for the Yankees helped turn around the ALCS opener despite young fan Jeffrey Meier reaching over the right-field wall where Baltimore's Tony Tarasco was set to catch the ball. MLB began using video for home run calls in 2008 and allowed challenges to ball/strike decisions starting this year.

# Yankees' season ends in 3-game sweep to the Rays in the ALDS

By STEPHEN WHYNO 

Thursday, October 8, 2026 3:36AM

NEW YORK -- Max Fried gave up two home runs, the New York Yankees had one taken off the board by fan interference and then their season ended Thursday night with a whimper.

After Anthony Volpe's would-be tying homer in the bottom of the sixth inning turned into a double on video review, the Yankees did not get a runner past second base. When leadoff hitter Trent Grisham struck out to end the ninth, it capped a 4-3 loss to the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 3 of the AL Division Series and a series sweep that extended the Yankees' championship drought to 17 years.

Without injured slugger Aaron Judge, they were one-hit and shut out in the opener, when catcher Austin Wells' baserunning blunder loomed large. Game 2 included four errors to get pushed to the brink of elimination.

The Yankees didn't go quietly — at least initially. When Fried gave up a run apiece in the third and fourth innings, the bats responded each time to tie the score.

Victor Mesa Jr. crushed Fried's 80th and final pitch for a go-ahead, two-run home run that was far from a short-porch homer like Ryan Vilade's earlier. It looked like New York would get it right back in a redemption moment for Volpe, but a Jeffrey Maier-esque moment came back to haunt the home team 30 years later.

With rookie George Lombard Jr. on base — and Wells would have been if not for a successful ABS challenge by the Rays — Volpe turned on right-hander Griffin Jax's 95.9 mph sinker and hit it 357 feet to left field. It was a matter of inches as to whether a fan reached over the fence and interfered with the ball or it would have cleared the wall entirely.

Called a home run by the umpires on the field, video review determined the fan did interfere. The replay official scored it an RBI double for Volpe with a run scored, but the run that did not turned out to be the difference.

With the air sucked out of Yankee Stadium, Spencer Jones — who singled and doubled in his first two plate appearances — struck out swinging to end the threat. The eighth started with Paul Goldschmidt reaching on a throwing error and finished with fellow pinch-hitter with Giancarlo Stanton striking out in just his second at-bat of the postseason.

Stanton got chances to swing the bat after strained calf muscles in each of his legs sidelined him since April 24. Judge was not afforded the same opportunity, left off the rosters for the AL Wild Card Series and the ALDS because of his calf injury.

Aaron Boone again fell short of a title in his ninth season as New York's manager, and some fans chanted "Fire Boone!" as they streamed to the exits.

# Rays beat Yankees for ALDS sweep behind Mesa homer, fan interference call

By 

The Canadian Press

Published: October 07, 2026 at 11:13p.m. EDT

Now Playing

01:28

Next Available Video Previous Available Video

NEW YORK (AP) — Victor Mesa Jr. hit a tiebreaking, two-run homer off Max Fried in the sixth inning, and the Tampa Bay Rays beat the New York Yankees 4-3 on Wednesday night with the help of a fan interference call for a three-game sweep of their AL Division Series.

Ryan Vilade also homered for the Rays, who reached the American League Championship Series for the first time since 2020 and host the Chicago White Sox or Cleveland Guardians in the opener on Monday.

After Mesa’s homer gave the Rays a 4-2 lead, Anthony Volpe appeared to hit a two-run shot against Griffin Jax with two outs in the bottom half as a fan reached over the left-field wall and caught the ball over the glove of a leaping Mesa.

A video review determined the ball would not have been over the wall and would not have been caught by Mesa. Volpe was awarded an RBI double and George Lombard Jr. was allowed to score from first. Jax recovered to strike out Spencer Jones.

Baseball’s adaptation of video technology was key to the inning.

Lombard reached with a one-out walk when a 3-1 pitch called a strike by plate umpire Dan Bellino was ruled inside on an ABS challenge. Austin Wells then walked on full-count changeup but an ABS challenge by Rays catcher Liam Hicks ruled the pitch caught the inside corner for a strikeout, bringing up Volpe.

Quite a change from 1996, when umpires did not have technology to assist and Derek Jeter’s homer for the Yankees helped turn around the ALCS opener despite Jeffrey Meier reaching over the right-field wall where Baltimore’s Tony Tarasco was set to catch the ball. MLB began using video for home run calls in 2008 and allowed challenges to ball/strike decisions starting this year.
